#4858. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4857. sonnen files for insolvency in Germany as US sales double

Residential battery storage maker sonnen is reporting two very different stories today: Its German business has filed for insolvency, while sonnen USA says sales have doubled and it’s preparing to expand.

The insolvency filing comes just two months after Shell sold sonnen to investment group TIVEN. Germany’s Handelsblatt reported that sonnen GmbH confirmed the filing and informed roughly 400 employees in Wildpoldsried, Bavaria, on October 22.

For homeowners with sonnen batteries, the immediate question is what happens to service. According to Handelsblatt, the company intends to keep supporting its more than 150,000 existing customers. But a substantial overhaul is coming: Numerous subsidiaries are expected to be wound down or enter insolvency proceedings under self-administration, with only one production site remaining. The report does not identify that site.

Meanwhile, sonnen USA’s announcement describes a growing home battery business. The company says sales have doubled and production has tripled year over year, supported by expanded manufacturing in Stone Mountain, Georgia. It expects to deliver more than 180 megawatt-hours of residential battery storage in 2026.

Much of that growth comes from virtual power plants (VPPs). These connect home batteries so they can work together to support the grid, giving households another way to earn value from their solar and storage systems.

In Texas, sonnen says its SOLRITE offering serves more than 6,000 homes, combining rooftop solar, batteries, energy management, and VPP participation. In Massachusetts, its sonnenCommunity program offers cash rewards to participating homeowners in National Grid and Eversource territories. The company also reports rising sales through its Wattsmart program in Utah.

TIVEN bought the entire global business, including sonnen USA. US CEO Blake Richetta stated today that “TIVEN is firmly committed to the long-term success of sonnen USA as a strong, market-leading company in the North American VPP energy market.”

TIVEN stated that it “looks forward to bolstering the company’s impressive growth.”

But the US announcement leaves an important question unanswered: How will the German restructuring affect the US operation and its customers? It doesn’t address the insolvency filing, and sonnen USA declined to comment on developments in Germany when contacted by pv magazine.

The US growth figures show demand for sonnen’s batteries. What customers still need is a clear explanation of how manufacturing, software support, and service will be maintained through the restructuring.

#4856. The Value of Appreciation

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Which is worth more: a million dollars today or a penny that doubles each day for 30 days?

At first, the million looks like the obvious choice.

The penny begins at one cent on day one and doubles each day afterward. By day 10, the balance is a measly $5.12. By day 20, the balance reaches a meager $5,242.88. By day 30, it reaches $5,368,709.12, more than five times the lump sum.

That is the power of compounding. Small beginnings can be easy to underestimate; early progress can look almost insignificant.

Everyday life also offers valuable moments that are easy to overlook: a small gesture of kindness, a moment of connection worth savoring, a heartfelt moment of gratitude.

These are psychological pennies: small acts of appreciation that are easy to take for granted but are worth repeating in pursuit of the good life. The invitation is to make appreciation a regular practice, rather than reserve it for one extraordinary occasion.What people usually think of as extraordinary is not likely to happen every day. Small reasons for gratitude offer more frequent opportunities to experience the benefits of appreciation. Waiting for something extraordinary can lead people to overlook the value already present in their lives.

Psychologists Mitchel Adler and Nancy Fagley define appreciation as “acknowledging the value and meaning of something—an event, a person, a behavior, an object—and feeling a positive emotional connection to it.” They identify eight aspects of appreciation, including gratitude, appreciation of the present moment, and awe.In finance, appreciation means an increase in value. A home or stock portfolio appreciates when its price rises.

The connection is a useful metaphor for psychological wealth. Recognizing value can increase the value people experience. An ordinary conversation with a friend can feel richer when someone recognizes the gift of having that person in their life. An ordinary afternoon can feel extraordinary when a person pauses to appreciate being alive and the opportunity to spend time with someone they love. In this sense, recognizing the value already present in relationships and experiences can increase how rich life feels.

In a 2012 study of 243 participants, psychologist Nancy Fagley found that appreciation was associated with greater life satisfaction. Awe offers one way to practice appreciation in ordinary life. Awe involves a sense of vastness that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world.A person does not necessarily need to visit the Grand Canyon or the Himalayas to experience awe. Someone might pause to consider the complexity of a living tree, witness an act of kindness, or feel a profound sense of wonder at a heart that keeps beating without conscious instruction.

In a small randomized study, psychologist Virginia Sturm and colleagues asked adults to take weekly 15-minute outdoor walks for eight weeks. One group also received instructions to approach their surroundings with wonder and seek out novelty. Compared with the control group, which received the walking assignment without those additional instructions, those encouraged to seek wonder and novelty reported greater increases over time in daily positive emotions involving connection with others.

To practice appreciation more consistently, choose a familiar activity and consider a more appreciative lens through which to view it.

Give one person your full attention. During a conversation with a friend or loved one, set aside distractions and appreciate the opportunity to spend time together. Listen with interest. When appropriate, let them know you are glad to have them in your life.

Reconsider something familiar. During a routine moment, notice something that is easy to take for granted. At a meal, that might be the nourishment the food provides, the people who made the meal possible, or the pleasure of tasting something you enjoy.

Take a walk with curiosity. During a walk, look closely at something you would usually pass by. Consider the complexity of a living tree, for example, or the scale of the sky above it. Allow time for curiosity and wonder.

The penny that began at one cent reaches $5.37 million by day 30. Psychological pennies can be just as easy to overlook, and compounding them over time may increase your psychological wealth. Small, ordinary moments can be worth doubling down on. Recognizing the value already present in such moments can increase how rich life feels.The practical idea is to return to such moments throughout the day and appreciate them more fully, rather than postpone appreciation until something extraordinary happens. There is no guaranteed rate of return in life satisfaction, but there are good reasons to invest consistently over the long run.

Those are investments that can be made today, and made again tomorrow.

#4855. Another megawatt-level charger enters China: 300 miles in 5 minutes

Chery has announced a 1.44 megawatt charging system, able to deliver 500km (311 miles) in 5 minutes. And it’s not even the fastest system available in China.

It’s become common knowledge at this point that Chinese EVs are the world’s state of the art, but the country isn’t sitting on its laurels, it’s still racing to compete with newer and better technology.

A case in point has been the country’s DC fast chargers, where we’ve seen a slew of announcements of new systems in just the last year.

BYD has a 1.5MW charger which it has already installed 10,000 of, Geely just announced a 2.2MW charger, and CATL has a hyper-fast charging battery.

The competition is so fierce that firms are starting to compete over seconds, not minutes of charging time.

And now, a new challenger appears: Chery.

Chery announced a 1.44MW charger that can add 500km (311miles) of range to a battery in 5 minutes, and can charge from 10-97% in 6 minutes and 50 seconds, as reported by CarNewsChina.

The numbers put it in league with the best of the best in the country. Per CarNewsChina’s accounting, the new Chery “Volt-Dragon” battery is the second-fastest at reaching 97% state of charge, 23 seconds behind CATL’s 6 minute, 27 second record time. FAW, Geely and BYD are all between 8 and 9 minutes for the same full charge metric.

Some other firms released times for charging in very cold or very warm weather, which Chery declined to release during its announcement. Though it did say that it could still deliver 500km of range in 8 minutes in “conservative scenarios.”

Could it be the drugged out Elon Musk is more into politics and taking over the world than advancing EV technology at an electric car company.

In Chery’s announcement, it dropped the same buzzword as Geely did: “AI-Powered.” Chery calls its system CheryMind, and supposedly it adjusts charging power based on temperature changes within the battery, to help maintain optimal charging speeds and battery health.

Meanwhile in the US, the fastest public chargers are around 400kW, with 750kW potentially coming next year. That’s all plenty quick enough for refueling, especially on a roadtrip, but for high-throughput DC charging locations, especially those in urban areas where some people might not have a consistent parking spot to charge in (and yes, we need to fix that), higher speed chargers can relieve a lot of pressure.

Chery has only just started installing chargers, and says it will have 100 chargers open in 10 Chinese cities soon. It plans to install 20,000 stations worldwide by 2029, which is quite a bit slower than BYD’s target to have 20,000 chargers installed by the end of this year.

#4854. It's So Much More Than Used Clothing

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

When I thought of Goodwill, I pictured used clothing. Then I toured its Miami-Dade facility and learned so much more.

Goodwill Industries of South Florida helps people with disabilities and other employment barriers gain greater independence through job training, employment, and placement services. According to president and CEO David Landsberg, it is Florida’s largest employer of people with disabilities and the 18th-largest employer in South Florida.

Its businesses include manufacturing military and other apparel, providing custodial services to federal workplaces, and operating a commercial laundry. They also provide career training in fields such as HVAC and solar installation and place graduates in community positions.

I was particularly moved by the employees making American flags for veterans’ burials. These flags will cover caskets for our veterans. I watched a blind man sew with remarkable precision and speed.

I saw enthusiasm and pride throughout the tour, especially during a Spirit of Goodwill Band rehearsal. The musicians, who work at Goodwill and have a variety of disabilities, were superb. They are given time during the workweek to practice, and they perform at community functions, including the organization’s fundraising gala.

Many of us carry disability insurance in case illness or injury prevents us from working. But what about someone born with a disability, or who developed one in childhood, who has never had the opportunity to work?

The World Health Organization’s 2022 guidelines recognize meaningful work as a source of confidence, accomplishment, and inclusion. Work gives our days structure, with tasks to complete and opportunities to grow. A conversation over lunch or someone asking how our weekend went may seem trivial until those interactions are missing, as many of us discovered during the pandemic.

As a parent who has spent decades advocating for my daughter and worrying about her future, I know how deeply reassuring it is to see an adult child take on work responsibilities and form relationships outside the family.

The Americans with Disabilities Act protects equal opportunity among qualified people with disabilities. Employers with 15 or more employees should not discriminate and should provide reasonable accommodations if the applicant can meet the job's qualifications. Yet, too many are unemployed.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, in 2025, the unemployment rate among people with disabilities ages 16 and older was 8.3 percent, compared with 4.1 percent among those without disabilities. Among people ages 16 to 64 with a disability, just 41.8 percent were working or looking for work in 2025.

Eileen Grubba, a disability activist, award-winning actress, writer, and producer, shared with me her valuable perspective: “Those with disabilities often have the most to offer. They have survived the unthinkable. We rarely consider what they handle every single day, and what they’ve learned because of it. We need to open our minds and turn to those who know best how to adapt, adjust, and overcome, simply because they’ve been overcoming all their lives."

Goodwill’s founder, Edgar J. Helms, expressed the organization’s guiding idea: “Not charity, but a chance.”

I left the tour thinking how little I knew about workplace accommodations and how heartwarming it is to see others succeed.

You might contact your local Goodwill or another employment organization and ask whether you can visit. A lot can be achieved through training, time, and connection.

#4853. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4849. The Law of Reversed Effort

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

For the better part of this decade, I suffered from a severe case of insomnia. Initially, it had biological origins. After coming down with COVID early in the pandemic, the virus triggered a rare autoimmune condition in me called Morvan syndrome. Morvan’s gift to its victims is profound, treatment-resistant insomnia (agrypnia excitata), and the syndrome can be fatal in up to 20 percent of reported cases. Fortunately (though it’s hard to diagnose), once it’s identified, it’s quite treatable. Unfortunately, prolonged insomnia can develop a learned psychological component, even after the original biological problem improves, so my sleepless nights continued even after IVIG immunotherapy resolved most of the other consequences of the condition.

So, as behavioral scientists often do, I was determined to solve my problem through intellect and science. I bought an Oura Ring and started tracking my sleep. I learned everything I could about sleep hygiene. I hired a sleep coach, therapist, and hypnotherapist. I got a silly pair of glasses and bought all the supplements. I even started injecting myself with peptides purported to help with sleep. Like so many who suffer from insomnia, I just wanted out of it. I jumped the shark when I bought a machine to freeze my prefrontal cortex, a machine so loud my poor wife was now not able to sleep either.

After more than five years of suffering, one little trick made it stop: I decided to stop caring. To be clear, I didn’t suddenly abandon my healthy sleep habits; I just stopped treating good sleep as something I needed to achieve.

If you follow my work, you know Alan Watts has been a significant influence in what I do. Although the law of reversed effort didn’t originate with him, he helped popularize similar ideas through his writing about Taoism and effortless action. Watts even described Lao-tzu as a master of the law of reversed effort.

Despite the name, the law of reversed effort is not a scientific law per se, in the same sense as something found in empirical disciplines. Rather, it’s a psychological idea that there are certain outcomes where increasing conscious effort begins to work against us. Sleep has emerged as the textbook example of this concept, but it shows up in a lot of places. For instance, the paradox of hedonism is the idea that the best way to become unhappy is to chase happiness (the foundation of my book, The Fun Habit). Or the ironic monitoring process, a topic extensively explored by psychologist Daniel Wegner, where in the pursuit of peace of mind, you inadvertently train yourself to subconsciously always scan for threats, therefore making peace of mind elusive.

Here’s how Wegner explains the monitoring process: When we deliberately try to create or suppress a mental state, two processes get activated. One tries to produce the outcome we want; the other monitors whether we are succeeding. Unfortunately, that monitoring process must keep looking for evidence of failure. For instance, if your goal is to stop feeling anxious, some part of your attention must continually ask, “Am I still anxious?”

In my case, with the goal of desperately wanting to fall asleep, my brain (unintentionally) was trained to keep noticing whether I was still awake. In fact, there’s even a sleep treatment that uses this paradox and reverses it. “Paradoxical intention” asks people with insomnia to let go of the effort to force sleep and, in some versions, gently try to stay awake instead. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that paradoxical intention improved important insomnia outcomes and reduced sleep-related performance anxiety (although the authors acknowledged that stronger research in this area is still needed).

For those of us like me who enjoy living in health metrics and data, optimization runs the risk of making problems worse. With sleep trackers now becoming ubiquitous, the problem has become so prevalent that researchers now have a term for it: orthosomnia. But hyperfocusing on a personal problem is hardly unique to sleep.

Both of my parents were professors who lived through the publish-or-perish era. Now that I better understand the pressures of that time, I’ve forgiven them for never being around. However, because there is a lot of residual pain from their absence, I’ve always felt a sense of duty to ensure that my children have all the access to me they need.

So, I read all the good parenting books and followed all the parenting influencers on social media; I tried to be the best parent I could be at every step. But beneath all those good intentions, a practice of rumination and a small “sub-agent of evaluation” began to emerge, framing our interactions as performative. In other words, every interaction with my kids was also an opportunity to collect data. Did I handle that correctly? Was I present enough? And even though I hate to admit this one: Do they like me?

Serendipitously, when my sleep miraculously improved, it dawned on me pretty quickly that I could apply the law of reversed effort to other areas of my life. So, I stopped worrying about being a good father (important to note, I didn’t stop being a good father). I was able to pull this off because I benefited from the confidence of knowing I had enough reps in to trust that the one-off disagreements and difficult afternoons were not a referendum. And once I stopped keeping score, something magical happened: I became more available to what was actually happening. The result is we all started having a lot more fun.

I can already see fans of Ryan Holiday’s work roll their eyes, so let me state the obvious: The law of reversed effort can be problematic if taken too far.Folks who truly know me understand that my argument is never for passivity or living a life of whimsy. On the contrary, direct effort works well for countless things. If you want to become stronger, you need to lift weights. If you want to learn a musical instrument, you need to practice. If you want deeper relationships, you need to put in the time.The important distinction to be aware of is between actions we can perform and states we’re trying to force, as well as becoming comfortable with not being wedded to an outcome. I can create a supportive environment in which to go to bed. I cannot command myself to sleep. I can listen carefully and be present with my children. I cannot force them to be endearing at every turn. I can flex my agency and autonomy to create time for enjoyable experiences. I can only order myself to become happy at my own peril.

Here’s a question I find myself asking more and more these days: Is this something I can directly affect? Or is this something more likely to emerge if I create the right conditions?

If you’ve gotten this far, I hope you see it was never about caring less. It’s about recognizing when your level of caring has quietly turned into an anxiety trap, because you’re trying to control something that is uncontrollable.

Some things respond beautifully when we push harder. Others seem to require us to create the right conditions, loosen our grip, and then simply allow them to happen. Learning this hasn’t just helped me improve my sleep. It’s made my life better by freeing up energy to be fully present with those I love and cherish. I’m excited to see where else I can benefit from the law of reversed effort as I apply it to other areas of my life. Stay tuned.

Ansfield, M. E., Wegner, D. M., & Bowser, R. (1996). Ironic effects of sleep urgency. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 34(7), 523–531. doi:10.1016/0005-7967(96)00031-9.

Baron, K. G., Abbott, S., Jao, N., Manalo, N., & Mullen, R. (2017). Orthosomnia: Are some patients taking the quantified self too far? Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 13(2), 351–354. doi:10.5664/jcsm.6472.

Espie, C. A., Broomfield, N. M., MacMahon, K. M., Macphee, L. M., & Taylor, L. M. (2006). The attention-intention-effort pathway in the development of psychophysiologic insomnia: a theoretical review. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 10(4), 215–245. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2006.03.002

Jansson-Fröjmark, M., Alfonsson, S., Bohman, B., Rozental, A., & Norell-Clarke, A. (2022). Paradoxical intention for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Sleep Research, 31(2), e13464. doi:10.1111/jsr.13464.

Masood, W., Lui, F., & Sitammagari, K. K. (2024). Morvan syndrome. In StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing.

Mauss, I. B., Tamir, M., Anderson, C. L., & Savino, N. S. (2011). Can seeking happiness make people unhappy? Paradoxical effects of valuing happiness. Emotion, 11(4), 807–815. doi:10.1037/a0022010.

Watts, A. W. (1951). The wisdom of insecurity: A message for an age of anxiety. Pantheon Books.

Wegner, D. M. (1994). Ironic processes of mental control. Psychological Review, 101(1), 34–52.

#4846. Overhead wired charging comes to Austin electric bus fleet

CapMetro’s Austin transit fleets electrified two public bus lines and opened two new park-and-ride facilities featuring overhead pantograph-style wired charging equipment to help Austinites breathe a little bit easier.

Originally announced in June, CapMetro’s two new park-and-ride stations are now open. Dubbed the Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center facilities debuted alongside the agency’s Rapid 800 and 837 electric bus routes, adding upgraded passenger amenities and end-of-line charging infrastructure to support its growing fleet of electric transit buses.

At CapMetro’s main bus depot, infrastructure partner Camber Charging supplied and installed two 1,440 kW charging systems connected to 48 industrial dispensers. The installation provides 2.9 MW of total charging capacity, and is designed to support overnight charging for up to 48 electric buses simultaneously.

The new Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center terminals extend that infrastructure along the Rapid 800 and 837 routes with the overhead pantograph chargers that are the big news here, allowing buses to top off their batteries at the end of each line and eliminate any lingering range anxiety for the trip back.

“Instead of a typical bus holding 8 hours of charging, on-route charging takes that out to 20 to 22 hours,” explains CapMetro Chief Operations Officer and Executive VP, Andy Skabowski. “Every time that pantograph drops, we charge that bus. That’s what makes a commitment like (every) 10- to 15-minute service possible.”

The buses themselves are built on Canadian manufacturer New Flyer’s Xcelsior battery-electric transit platform (battery specs aren’t included in the release, but New Flyer claims up to 660 kWh of available capacity). And, with up to 320 all-electric hp with all its torque available at 0 rpm, the city’s 48 electric buses will have no problem navigating Austin’s stop-and-go traffic.

This seems like a logical cost effective solution. In theory, this should enable transit systems to purchase busses with smaller batteries which would surely offset the cost of the new charging infrastructure.

Camber Charging provides preventive maintenance, charger and energy management software and remote diagnostics across all three locations.

#4845. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4844. The Powerful Impact of Social Comparisons in Everyday Life

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

"Did she do that? Did she do that?" said the mother of my daughter's friend, her eyes wide and her jaw dropped — her entire system in a state of shock.

She had just arrived at the daycare center to pick up her daughter. Near the entrance was a chalkboard where the kids were encouraged to draw unrestricted.

Some minutes earlier, my daughter and her daughter had both been drawing stick figures. I had arrived early, and my daughter had pleaded with me to "draw some people." However, the daycare center had a strict policy against parents helping their kids; kids should develop independence while at the center.

Gently, I reminded her that I wasn't allowed to help, but she persisted. And so after checking that no staff members were watching, I made quick drawings of a couple of kids. They were barely passable, but next to her daughter's stick figures, they were Da Vincis.

I had just returned the chalk to my daughter, who was now busily applying some final touches, when the other girl's mom showed up. The two drawings contrasted sharply, leaving a powerful impression on the mom. But what could I say? I had violated the center's rules.

I had to put the mom out of her misery. Under my breath, I said, "No, no, I drew them. She begged me to do it. Don't tell anyone."

Echoing the two masks of Greek theater, her face shifted from tragedy to a kind of joy.

Why did she feel this comparison so keenly?

A few details explain this. My daughter and her friend were the same age (4) and gender. They also had the same birthday. Similarity in related attributes increases the impact of social comparisons. If her friend were a boy and a year older, the mother might have brushed off the comparison; it lacked relevance. Parents often zero in on attributes for a sense of how a comparison should register, especially at these early ages when a year or more can be especially important in determining achievement.

I often think of this episode. To me, it captures how social comparisons affect people in everyday life.

How we stack up with others often has deciding consequences for success in important areas of life, from work to romance, and for the feelings about self that follow from these outcomes. Part of growing up and maturing as adults is about assessing strengths and weaknesses largely determined by relative standing, grappling with the emotional and practical implications of such assessments, and making life choices guided by this process.

And, of course, our kids are extensions of ourselves.

In my experience, I can think of no better example of these truths than this small but telling incident occurring in my daughter’s pre-school.

#4841. Yozma IN 11 review: The OG mini e-moto gets updates galore

…including 4.5kW motor, bigger 1.4kWh battery and 45mph top speed

Yozma may not have invented the mini moto space, but they certainly helped mainstream it. Together with Tuttios and Sur Rons, Yozma’s IN10 was one of the most popular mini motos out there, and if you surveyed the average group of 14-15-year-olds in a suburban rideout, you’d be hard-pressed not to find at least a few Yozma IN10s among them…

Today Yozma is shipping the IN 11 ($100 off with code 9TO5TOYS100), which attempts to bridge the gap between entry-level mini-bikes and high-end off-roaders, but at what cost?

Taken in a vacuum, the Yozma IN11 is an impressive update to the IN 10 and actually is more closely specced to the bigger IN10 Pro.

But we of course, don’t live in a vacuum, and others, including the Heybike Villain and the Engwe Eagle have already brought 52V, 4.5kW motors to the pit bike form factor, sometimes at much lower cost.

I should say here that parents who want to keep their kids’ e-motos in the 20-30mph range are going to be a whole lot happier with the 2.6kW than 4.5kW motors. Two nice safety improvements over the original Yozma IN10 include the magnetic kill switch and brake lights on the IN11.

If we are keeping it real here, there are dozens of similar-sized and spec’d mini-e-motos out there, often at a much lower cost than the Yozma IN11. But I’d argue that as the biggest and most trusted of these brands, Yozma is a safer bet.

Also, the IN11 is just a lot more solid than the random Amazon/Alibaba electric pit bike. Putting the IN11 together is quicker and easier than any other emoto I’ve built, and it just feels a lot more solid.

That feeling extends to the safety features. The brakes are more dialed in. The turning feels a lot tighter, and the overall ride is quieter and lighter. I believe, and my limited testing bears this out, that spec for spec, I got a lot more range on the IN11 than I got on other bikes with similar battery and motor specs. That 200nm of torque feels like it belongs on a much more expensive e-moto.

The smart wheelie mode is a nice trick (15, 25, or 40 degrees wheelie settings) and something we’ve only seen on Anylands for this price point so far. It is less of a standout feature on the IN11, and we expect to see this on just about every new pit bike coming out over the next few years. In fact, we’ve got another one in the review queue now.

That said, the price, which is currently fluctuating between $1299 and $1499 (don’t forget your $100 off 9TO5TOYS100 code), Yozma is going to be on the more expensive side of the 4.5kW emotos out there and some of the less established and more sketchy newcomers are bringing an intense value competition to the place where Yozma once dominated by itself.

#4840. When Stress Drives Us to the Bathroom

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

“I have a new philosophy. I'm only going to dread one day at a time.” —Charles Schulz

Stress can drive many people to the bathroom. That stress can come in the form of an overbearing boss, an abusive partner, or just bad news. These people are wired to redirect stress to their gut, and more specifically, defecation. Welcome to anxiety poop.

Just seeing something stressful can make many of us nauseated. You don’t need to actually ride a rickety roller coaster; just looking at it can provide a frisson of anxiety.

You may think you don’t have this issue, but everyone has a strong gut-brain connection. Before a presentation, we get butterflies in our stomach. When we have to make quick decisions under stress, we defer to our gut feelings. When we have to do something difficult, it can be gut-wrenching.

But how is the brain connected to the gut?

Anxiety poop is a great example of the gut-brain axis at work. Stress, whether caused by the outside environment or internal microbes, causes serotonin to be released in the gut. That induces peristalsis and an urge to find a bathroom STAT. Not fun, but also not uncommon.

Dialed up high enough, anxiety puts out an all-points bulletin to the body. It affects the fight-or-flight response (sympathetic), as well as the rest-and-digest response (parasympathetic).

The sympathetic fight-or-flight response is wired to the brain via spinal nerves. When triggered, we produce adrenalin and cortisol — the stress drugs — which push us to hulk out, either to fight or run.

Meanwhile, the parasympathetic rest-and-digest system is wired to the brain by the vagus nerve. When this response is triggered, special cells lining the gut secrete serotonin.

We typically think of serotonin as a chemical messenger in the brain. That’s what SSRIs target. But 90% of your serotonin is in your gut, and it doesn’t act like an antidepressant. Instead, it’s in charge of peristalsis, the rhythmic constrictions that pulse your food through the gut. Under stress, a lot of serotonin is released, pulsing your food with a vengeance.

Why has evolution fashioned such behavior?

There are two good reasons: One is the need for speed. If a tiger starts to chase you, you drop what you’re holding and run. For some extra weight loss, your body uses the serotonin technique to evacuate your bowels, making you lighter on your feet. Embarrassment can come later, if you survive the tiger. As a bonus, the energy you would have spent on digestion is now available for sprinting.

This is great for dealing with tigers, but less-than-suitable for menacing bosses or spouses. Constantly being in this state of hypervigilance can damage your gut lining, especially since the fight-or-flight response has usurped all the blood meant for the gut.

The second evolutionary reason is because your anxiety circuits have been repurposed for food poisoning. You have cells in your gut that can detect an invasion by pathogens. They communicate this info to the brain which decides, based on the strength of the signal, whether to purge or not. It tends to err on the dramatic side, and a severe bout of food poisoning will cause speedy evacuation from both ends of the digestive tract.

These two signals of stress—one from the outside and one from the inside—are handled by the same brain circuits. Nature is frugal, and she loves to repurpose anatomy. One way or another, anxiety is going to disrupt your gut.

That makes this circuitry cyclic: A disturbed gut can create anxiety, and anxiety can disturb the gut. This can lead to chronic conditions like IBS, Crohn’s, IBD, and gastric reflux. Over time, it can snowball into systemic inflammation, threatening the health of all your other organs.

This vicious cycle can be tamed, however, into a virtuous cycle. There are some do’s and some don’ts:

We have little control over our external stress, although some people find meditating can help them deal with a crazy world. But we have plenty of control over our diet and exercise.

It can be hard to break habits—who wants to voluntarily quit candy or cocktails?—but the payoff is surprisingly large. Once your microbiome is happy, it becomes harder to perturb. A healthy gut can fend off pathogens better than your immune system can. That builds resilience and lowers your natural anxiety.

And all of that can keep you from pooping your pants under stress. So give it a try.

Breit, Sigrid, Aleksandra Kupferberg, Gerhard Rogler, and Gregor Hasler. “Vagus Nerve as Modulator of the Brain–Gut Axis in Psychiatric and Inflammatory Disorders.” Frontiers in Psychiatry 9 (March 2018): 44. doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2018.00044.

Herselman, Mauritz F., Sheree Bailey, and Larisa Bobrovskaya. “The Effects of Stress and Diet on the ‘Brain–Gut’ and ‘Gut–Brain’ Pathways in Animal Models of Stress and Depression.” International Journal of Molecular Sciences 23, no. 4 (2022): 2013. doi.org/10.3390/ijms23042013.

Foster, Jane A., Linda Rinaman, and John F. Cryan. “Stress & the Gut-Brain Axis: Regulation by the Microbiome.” Neurobiology of Stress 7 (March 2017): 124–36. doi.org/10.1016/j.ynstr.2017.03.001.

#4839. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4836. The Hidden Dynamics Shaping Our Relationships

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

In the words often attributed to the Buddha, “Nothing ever exists entirely alone; everything is in relation to everything else.”

Consider a tree. It can only grow by drawing nutrients from the soil below while relying on rain and sunlight from above. Its roots interact with fungi and microorganisms underground, while its branches provide shelter and nourishment for other living things.

We humans are no different. Our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors don't exist in isolation. They are continually shaped by our relationships and environments. In turn, our own actions, words, tone of voice, and body language influence the people around us, often in ways we don't immediately recognize.

Understanding this interconnectedness is a core competency of spiritual intelligence. [i] It also offers a practical way to understand why we sometimes find ourselves repeating the same frustrating patterns in our relationships, families, and everyday lives.

My appreciation for systems thinking began during my junior year at MIT in a class taught by organizational theorist Peter Senge.[ii]

Systems thinking invites us to look beyond individual events and recognize the larger networks of relationships in which they occur.[iii] Every action produces reactions elsewhere, and those reactions feed back into the system again. Of course, we only discussed this framework in the context of business, operations, and leadership, but I was immediately struck by how much this perspective explained about human behavior on the whole.

I see it all the time in the couples I counsel. One partner feels unheard and raises their voice in frustration. The other gets defensive and withdraws, protecting themselves. That withdrawal makes the first partner feel more ignored, so they try even harder and more forcefully to break through the "wall," only perpetuating the cycle. From either person's perspective, the problem may appear to be the other's behavior. But when we look at the relationship as a system, we begin to see something different: each person's response is influencing the other's, creating a loop that neither necessarily intends.

It made sense to me to learn that such system dynamics and feedback loops are the heart of several attachment-based couples therapy modalities such as Psychobiological Approach to Couple Therapy (PACT)[iv] and Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT)[v].

At the heart of systems thinking are two fundamental dynamics: positive and negative feedback loops. Despite their names, positive and negative don't necessarily mean good or bad.

Negative feedback loops stabilize a system, like a thermostat adjusting the temperature in a room. Positive feedback loops, meanwhile, reinforce existing patterns, whether healthy or unhealthy. Appreciation can breed more appreciation, just as frustration can breed more frustration.

Consider what happens when someone close to you expresses genuine appreciation for something you've done. You feel seen and valued, which may inspire you to be more generous or attentive in return. Your response makes the other person feel appreciated, too.

Unfortunately, the reverse is equally possible. Imagine walking into the kitchen and seeing that your partner has left dirty dishes all over the counter. You gripe, "Why do you always leave your dishes for me to clean?" Formulated as a question, through a frustrated tone of voice, this statement is likely to be interpreted by your partner as a criticism. They get defensive and a fight ensues. Alternatively, a more authentic and vulnerable response might sound like, "I am feeling exhausted and disconnected, and I need your help in keeping our space clean. Would you be willing to put your dishes in the dishwasher when done?”

These patterns can become so familiar that we stop noticing them. We begin to see our partner as defensive, or intrusive, our child as difficult, or our friend as inconsiderate, without recognizing how our own reactions may be contributing to the very behaviors that frustrate us.

One of the most powerful lessons of systems thinking is that changing even one part of a system can alter the entire dynamic.

Suppose your child is struggling with schoolwork. Your frequent reminders to study could feel like pressure, making them more resistant, and their procrastination will only increase your frustration. Instead of pushing harder, you might ask what's making the work difficult. Responding with curiosity rather than frustration can help break the cycle.

This is where spiritual intelligence becomes especially valuable. Understanding our interconnectedness and interdependence, along with qualities such as self-awareness, compassion, humility, and presence, can help us recognize our automatic reactions and choose how we want to respond.

A useful exercise is to map the feedback loops operating in one of your important relationships.

Think of a recurring interaction, particularly one that leaves you feeling frustrated or misunderstood, and ask yourself:

Try approaching these questions with curiosity rather than blame. We’re not looking to accuse; we’re looking to diagnose and understand the system at play.

You can also examine relationships where you feel particularly supported. What patterns of behavior make those relationships work, and how might you recreate them elsewhere?

Systems thinking reminds us that every interaction contributes, however subtly, to the conditions in which our relationships develop. Something as simple as a moment of patience can interrupt a familiar cycle of conflict and create room for a different response.

We may not be able to control how others behave, but we can become more conscious of what we contribute to the systems we share. And sometimes, that small change is enough to set something much larger in motion.

[i] Malik, M. S., & Tariq, S. (2016). Impact of spiritual intelligence on organizational performance. International Review of Management and Marketing, 6(2), 289-297. https://izlik.org/JA55AE55NC

[ii] Senge, P. M. (1990). The fifth discipline: The art and practice of the learning organization. Doubleday.

[iii] Behl, D. V., & Ferreira, S. (2014). Systems thinking: An analysis of key factors and relationships. Procedia Computer Science, 36, 104–109. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2014.09.045

[iv] Tatkin, S. (2009). A psychobiological approach to couple therapy: Integrating attachment and personality theory as interchangeable structural components. Psychologist-Psychoanalyst, 29(3), 7–15.

[v] Johnson, S. M., & Best, M. (2003). A systemic approach to restructuring adult attachment: The EFT model of couples therapy. In P. Erdman & T. Caffery (Eds.), Attachment and family systems: Conceptual, empirical and therapeutic relatedness (pp. 165–192). Routledge.

#4834. Tesla’s $10B solar factory could get 35 years of tax breaks in Texas

Tesla’s proposed $10 billion “Project Crystal Sun” solar factory in Texas could get up to 35 years of local tax breaks on its equipment, according to the four agreements Fort Bend County commissioners approved on Thursday.

The vote was 4-0. And Tesla still hasn’t committed to building the plant in Texas.

As we first reported in August, Tesla applied for a 10-year school property tax limitation under the state’s JETI program, through Lamar CISD and the Texas Comptroller. The plan is a vertically integrated solar plant near Richmond, southwest of Houston, that would make everything from silicon ingots to finished modules, with commercial production targeted for Q1 2029.

Lamar CISD approved the school tax piece in September. The county was next.

On October 22, the commissioners court approved items 25A to 25D on its agenda: a Chapter 312 tax abatement, a Chapter 381 incentive agreement, a foreign trade zone agreement with a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT), and a “true up” PILOT agreement. Interim County Judge Daniel Wong abstained because his engineering firm has worked with Tesla.

Each agreement covers a different slice of Tesla’s tax bill, and together they run for decades.

The Chapter 312 agreement abates 100% of county property taxes on Tesla’s equipment and other tangible personal property at the plant for 10 tax years. The clock starts in tax year 2029 by default, but Tesla can move it to the first year after production starts, as late as 2031 without needing the county’s approval.

Tesla’s JETI application splits the $10.1 billion into $1.52 billion of real property and $8.6 billion of personal property, mostly production equipment.

Land and buildings aren’t part of the deal. Anything that isn’t eligible for the abatement, including the land and buildings, stays “fully taxable at all times,” according to the agreement.

Inventory goes through the foreign trade zone deal instead. Tesla’s site would be part of Port Freeport’s Foreign-Trade Zone No. 149, which exempts eligible inventory from local property tax. In exchange for the county not objecting, Tesla agreed to make PILOT payments, set at “zero dollars or 0%” of the forgone taxes for as long as the abatement is in effect.

When the abatement ends, the Chapter 381 agreement takes over. Tesla starts paying county taxes on its equipment, and the county pays 90% of them back as an annual grant for 20 years. The county keeps 10% for its general fund.

Inventory follows the same pattern. After the abatement, Tesla’s FTZ payment rises to 10% of the taxes that would otherwise apply.

There’s one more lever. If Tesla averages at least 12,000 employees for any two consecutive years during the first decade, the first five years of the rebate period become a 100% grant, and the rebate period stretches from 20 to 25 years.

That pushes the agreement out to Project Year 35. It’s also 2,288 jobs above the 9,712 Tesla says it will create.

To keep the tax breaks, Tesla has to start construction by June 30, 2027, begin “regular commercial production of solar cells” by December 31, 2030, and invest $10 billion by the later of December 31, 2031 or two years after production starts. Force majeure and “ERCOT Delay” provisions can extend those dates.

The jobs ramp is 2,500, 5,000, 7,500, then 9,712 employees by the fourth year of operations, with an average compensation of $55 per hour. Tesla gets the full abatement as long as it hits 90% of the headcount target, which is about 8,741 people.

The penalties are mild. Missing a jobs or wage target for one year only costs Tesla that year’s break, and two misses in a row lets the county terminate the agreement. Full recapture of abated taxes, plus a possible 15% penalty if they aren’t repaid within 60 days, is reserved for “Material Defaults” like missing the $10 billion investment, blowing the construction deadlines or abandoning the plant for 12 months.

Under the Chapter 381 deal, grants from earlier years can’t be clawed back for a headcount shortfall.

The county’s floor is small. The true-up agreement only guarantees that Fort Bend collects at least $2 million a year, and 25% of the taxes Tesla pays on its real property, the county’s 10% share and the FTZ payments all count toward that total.

For scale, Tesla’s own consultant, Kroll, estimated in the JETI filing that the project would pay $276.5 million in Fort Bend County general taxes over 38 years without incentives, peaking at $16.2 million in 2030. That estimate lumps land, buildings and equipment together. The equipment portion is the one the county just agreed to give back, for most of those years.

In its application, it says the economics of the Fort Bend site are “not competitive” with an unnamed site in another state without the JETI limitation and local abatements. The competing state is redacted in a confidential supplement.

None of the documents state a production capacity. The only big number is a quote from Elon Musk at Davos in January, cited in the application: “The SpaceX and Tesla team, both separately, are working to build to 100 GW a year of solar power in the U.S., of manufactured solar power.”

For comparison, Qcells is spending $2.5 billion on its ingot-to-module campus in Cartersville, Georgia, where a 3.5 GW cell line started production this year. Crystal Sun’s budget is four times that.

Tesla has been here before. New York spent $950 million on the Buffalo factory for Tesla’s solar business, and when the solar plans fell apart, Tesla turned to things other than solar to meet its employment requirements, including data labeling for Autopilot. Tesla did announce production of a new solar panel in Buffalo last year.

We want this factory to happen. A US plant making its own ingots, wafers, cells and modules would be rare, and it’s one of the few parts of Tesla’s business that still lines up with the mission it used to talk about before its “awesome abundance” pivot based on AI.

But corporate America loves its tax breaks. For 10 years, Tesla pays no county tax on the $8.6 billion of equipment that makes up most of the project. For the next 20, it gets 90% of it back. In return, the county’s guaranteed minimum is $2 million a year, on a $10 billion plant. And Tesla still hasn’t said it’s coming.

That’s how site selection works now. Companies file, collect offers from several states, and the county that bids the most wins. Fort Bend’s economic development director, Carlos Guzman, told ABC13 the county “would’ve been eliminated from consideration” without these agreements. Hard to argue with that, and it’s exactly why these deals keep getting richer.

That bonus for extra workers looks like an invitation to gaming (if things get that far). Paying people for make-work for a couple of years could yield tax breaks well exceeding their combined wages.

The protections are thin too. One bad year costs Tesla a year of breaks, and past rebates can’t be clawed back over a headcount shortfall, even though the county’s goal is obviously long-term employment.

Then there’s the equipment. Reuters reported in March that Tesla was in talks to buy $2.9 billion of Chinese solar equipment, and its supply chain is already caught in a patent fight between Chinese suppliers.

The state still has to sign off on the school-tax piece. After that, it’s on Tesla. Is it actually building in Texas, or is Fort Bend’s offer just leverage against the other state? From what I’m hearing, Tesla is set on the Houston-area location.

Tesla wants to start making solar panels in Texas by 2029, but you don’t have to wait that long to go solar at home.
